stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A textile museum owns 1,200 hand-stitched quilts made between 1850 and 1900. A conservator chose 80 of these quilts at random and measured the quilting stitches on each one. The 80 quilts had a mean of 9.4 stitches per inch, with an associated margin of error of 0.6 stitches per inch.
choices: Every quilt in the museum's collection plausibly has between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean for all quilts made in the United States from 1850 to 1900 is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean for all 1,200 quilts in the museum's collection is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean for the 80 quilts the conservator measured is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
explanation: The interval is $9.4 - 0.6 = 8.8$ to $9.4 + 0.6 = 10.0$ stitches per inch. A margin of error describes where the population mean plausibly lies. The population here is the one the sample came from, which is the museum's 1,200 quilts. So the mean stitch density of the whole collection is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0.

A.why: You applied the interval to individual quilts. It is a range for the collection's mean, and individual quilts can fall well outside it.

B.why: You generalized beyond the population that was sampled. The 80 quilts came only from this museum's collection, so the result can't speak for every American quilt from the period.

D.why: You applied the interval to the sample instead of the population. The conservator measured those 80 quilts directly, so their mean is known to be exactly 9.4. The margin of error describes uncertainty about the 1,200 quilts.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A county health department surveyed 500 adults chosen at random from the county's residents. Of those surveyed, 38% reported getting a flu vaccine during the most recent season. The associated margin of error for this estimate is 4%.
choices: It is plausible that between 34% and 42% of the 500 surveyed adults got a flu vaccine last season.
It is plausible that between 34% and 42% of all adults in the county got a flu vaccine last season.
It is not possible that more than 42% of all adults in the county got a flu vaccine last season.
About 4% of the surveyed adults likely gave incorrect answers about getting a flu vaccine last season.
explanation: The interval is $38\% - 4\% = 34\%$ to $38\% + 4\% = 42\%$. It estimates the proportion for the population that was sampled, which is all adults in the county. So it is plausible that between 34% and 42% of the county's adults were vaccinated.

A.why: You applied the interval to the sample. The department knows that exactly 38% of the 500 respondents said yes. The uncertainty is about the whole county.

C.why: You treated the interval as a hard boundary. A margin of error gives a plausible range, so values outside it are unlikely but still possible. 'Not possible' claims too much certainty.

D.why: You read the margin of error as the share of respondents who answered wrongly. It measures sampling variability: how far the estimate could plausibly be from the true county proportion.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: Biologists measured 60 green sea turtles chosen at random from those nesting on Isla Corva during one season. The mean carapace length of the 60 turtles was 98 centimeters, with an associated margin of error of 3 centimeters.
choices: Most green sea turtles nesting on Isla Corva that season plausibly had carapace lengths between 95 and 101 centimeters.
The mean carapace length of all green sea turtles worldwide is plausibly between 95 and 101 centimeters.
It is not plausible that the mean carapace length of the turtles nesting on Isla Corva that season was above 98 centimeters.
The mean carapace length of all green sea turtles nesting on Isla Corva that season is plausibly between 95 and 101 centimeters.
explanation: The interval is $98 - 3 = 95$ to $98 + 3 = 101$ centimeters. The turtles were sampled from those nesting on Isla Corva that season, so the conclusion covers the mean carapace length of that population and nothing larger.

A.why: You applied the interval to individual turtles. It describes the population mean and says nothing about where most individual lengths fall. Individual lengths could vary far more than 3 centimeters.

B.why: You generalized beyond the population sampled. Turtles from one beach in one season can't represent green sea turtles worldwide.

C.why: You treated the estimate of 98 as if it were exact. Any value from 98 up to 101 is inside the plausible range, so a mean above 98 is entirely plausible.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A city planning office surveyed 400 households chosen at random in Ward 3. The mean one-way commute time for these households was 34 minutes, with an associated margin of error of 5 minutes. A transit agency report claims that the mean one-way commute time for Ward 3 households is 40 minutes.
choices: The claim is unlikely to be accurate, because 40 minutes is outside the plausible range for the Ward 3 mean.
The claim is plausible, because 40 minutes is within the margin of error of the survey's estimate of 34 minutes.
The claim is unlikely to be accurate, because no Ward 3 household has a commute longer than 39 minutes.
The claim is unlikely to be accurate, and the mean commute for the whole city is also less than 40 minutes.
explanation: The plausible range for the Ward 3 mean is $34 - 5 = 29$ to $34 + 5 = 39$ minutes. The value 40 is above that range, so the agency's claim about the Ward 3 mean is unlikely. Your conclusion has to stay about the mean and about Ward 3 only.

B.why: You made an arithmetic slip. The difference is $40 - 34 = 6$ minutes, which is more than the 5-minute margin of error, so 40 is outside the interval.

C.why: You applied the interval to individual households. The 29-to-39 range is for the Ward 3 mean, and plenty of individual households could commute longer than 39 minutes.

D.why: You extended the result to a population that was never sampled. Only Ward 3 households were surveyed, so the data say nothing about the citywide mean.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An ecologist marked off a 20-hectare meadow into square-meter plots and chose 50 of those plots at random. She counted the milkweed stems in each chosen plot. The mean was 14 stems per plot, with an associated margin of error of 3 stems per plot.
choices: Every square-meter plot in the meadow plausibly contains between 11 and 17 milkweed stems.
The mean number of milkweed stems per square-meter plot in the meadow is plausibly between 11 and 17.
The mean number of milkweed stems per square-meter plot in the meadow is plausibly between 14 and 17.
The mean number of milkweed stems per square-meter plot in every meadow in the region is plausibly between 11 and 17.
explanation: The interval runs from $14 - 3 = 11$ to $14 + 3 = 17$ stems. The plots were sampled from this one meadow, so the interval gives plausible values for the mean number of stems per plot across the whole meadow.

A.why: You applied the interval to every individual plot. It describes the meadow-wide mean. Single plots could have far fewer or far more stems.

C.why: You only added the margin of error. A margin of error extends both ways from the estimate, so the interval also runs down to $14 - 3 = 11$.

D.why: You extended the result beyond the population sampled. Every plot came from one meadow, so the data can't describe other meadows in the region.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A textile historian randomly selected 60 of the 1,200 pre-1900 quilts held by a regional museum and measured the stitch density of each one. From the sample, the estimated mean stitch density was 9.4 stitches per inch, with an associated margin of error of 0.6 stitch per inch.
choices: It is plausible that the mean stitch density of all pre-1900 quilts in the museum is between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
Every pre-1900 quilt in the museum has a stitch density between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
It is plausible that the mean stitch density of all quilts made before 1900, in any collection, is between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean stitch density of all pre-1900 quilts in the museum is greater than 9.4 stitches per inch.
explanation: You compute $9.4 - 0.6 = 8.8$ and $9.4 + 0.6 = 10.0$. The margin of error gives a plausible range for the population mean. The population is the 1,200 pre-1900 quilts the sample was drawn from, so the mean stitch density for that collection is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.

B.why: You applied the interval to each quilt instead of to the mean. The margin of error describes where the population mean plausibly lies. It says nothing about the range of individual quilts, and some quilts can fall well outside it.

C.why: You computed the right interval but extended it to a population that was never sampled. The quilts were drawn only from this one museum's collection, so the conclusion covers only that collection.

D.why: You made a one-sided claim that the data can't support. The interval runs from 8.8 to 10.0, so the population mean could just as plausibly be below 9.4 as above it.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A musicologist randomly selected 200 of the 3,000 hymns in a church archive. Of the sampled hymns, 38% were written in triple meter. The associated margin of error for this estimate is 5 percentage points.
choices: It is plausible that between 66 and 86 hymns in the archive are written in triple meter.
It is plausible that between 990 and 1,290 hymns in the archive are written in triple meter.
Exactly 1,140 hymns in the archive are written in triple meter.
It is plausible that between 1,135 and 1,145 hymns in the archive are written in triple meter.
explanation: The plausible range for the percent is $38\% - 5\% = 33\%$ to $38\% + 5\% = 43\%$. You apply that range to all 3,000 hymns in the archive: $0.33 \times 3{,}000 = 990$ and $0.43 \times 3{,}000 = 1{,}290$. So it is plausible that between 990 and 1,290 hymns in the archive are in triple meter.

A.why: You applied the interval to the 200 sampled hymns ($0.33 \times 200 = 66$ and $0.43 \times 200 = 86$) instead of the 3,000 hymns in the archive. The estimate is about the whole archive, so you need to multiply by 3,000.

C.why: You treated the estimate as exact. $0.38 \times 3{,}000 = 1{,}140$ is the single best guess, but the margin of error means the true count is uncertain, so 'exactly' claims too much.

D.why: You treated the margin of error as 5 hymns and wrote $1{,}140 \pm 5$. The margin is 5 percentage points of the archive, which is $0.05 \times 3{,}000 = 150$ hymns.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: Astronomers randomly selected 80 stars from a catalog of 2,500 red dwarf stars and measured how long each star takes to rotate once. From the sample, the estimated mean rotation period was 42 days, with an associated margin of error of 7 days.
choices: Most red dwarf stars in the catalog have a rotation period between 35 days and 49 days.
It is plausible that the mean rotation period of the red dwarf stars in the catalog is between 35 days and 49 days.
The mean rotation period of the red dwarf stars in the catalog is certainly greater than 35 days.
The rotation periods of the red dwarf stars in the catalog differ from 42 days by at most 7 days.
explanation: You compute $42 - 7 = 35$ and $42 + 7 = 49$. The margin of error gives a plausible range for the mean rotation period of the population, which is the 2,500 catalog stars the sample came from. So the catalog's mean rotation period is plausibly between 35 and 49 days.

A.why: You applied the interval to individual stars. It describes the population mean, not where most stars' periods fall. Individual rotation periods can vary far more widely than the mean does.

C.why: You turned a plausible range into a certainty. A margin of error doesn't rule out values outside the interval with certainty, so 'certainly' overstates what the sample shows.

D.why: You read the margin of error as the spread of the individual measurements. It measures uncertainty in the estimated mean. It doesn't measure how far each star's period is from 42 days.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An ecologist divided a wetland preserve into 900 plots of equal area and randomly selected 50 of them. Counts in the selected plots gave an estimated mean of 14.6 frog egg masses per plot, with an associated margin of error of 2.8 egg masses.
choices: It is plausible that the mean number of egg masses per plot in the preserve is 12.
Every plot in the preserve contains between 11.8 and 17.4 frog egg masses.
The mean number of egg masses per plot in the preserve is exactly 14.6.
It is plausible that the mean number of egg masses per plot in all regional wetlands is 12.
explanation: You compute $14.6 - 2.8 = 11.8$ and $14.6 + 2.8 = 17.4$. The population mean for the preserve's 900 plots is plausibly anywhere from 11.8 to 17.4. Since 12 is in that interval, a mean of 12 egg masses per plot in the preserve is plausible.

B.why: You applied the interval to every individual plot. The interval is about the mean count per plot. Individual plots can have many more or many fewer egg masses.

C.why: You treated the sample estimate as the exact population value. 14.6 is the sample's estimate, and the margin of error of 2.8 shows the true mean is uncertain.

D.why: You found a value inside the interval but extended the conclusion beyond the population sampled. Only plots in this one preserve were sampled, so the result says nothing about other wetlands in the region.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A print curator randomly selected 120 of the 2,400 woodblock prints in a printshop's archive. Of the sampled prints, 15% showed visible registration errors, where colors were misaligned. The associated margin of error for this estimate is 4 percentage points.
choices: It is plausible that between 11% and 19% of the prints in the archive show registration errors.
About 4% of the sampled prints were wrongly classified as having or lacking registration errors.
It is plausible that between 11% and 19% of all woodblock prints ever made show registration errors.
It is certain that more than 11% of the prints in the archive show registration errors.
explanation: You compute $15\% - 4\% = 11\%$ and $15\% + 4\% = 19\%$. The sample was drawn at random from this archive's 2,400 prints, so the percent of prints in the archive with registration errors is plausibly between 11% and 19%.

B.why: You read the margin of error as the percent of prints that were misclassified. A margin of error measures sampling uncertainty in the estimate. It doesn't count mistakes in judging individual prints.

C.why: You computed the right interval but applied it to a population that was never sampled. The prints came only from this one printshop's archive, so the conclusion can't extend to all woodblock prints.

D.why: You made a one-sided, certain claim. The interval makes values from 11% to 19% plausible, but it doesn't make anything certain, and a one-sided claim ignores the upper bound.
